**Before the appointment**
- Put the appointment date in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how complete your notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Keep it to three or four.
- Make your notes for the past 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over the first page or show it. It is made to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can make the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

It is a summary of what you entered, plus what you yourself added from the Health app. It is not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record, and any patterns in it are coincidence checks, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask questions that the notes do not answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add new medication with the start date. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries from before and after, and that makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single moment in time: the day on which you have not had a period for 12 months in a row, if there is no other explanation for it (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries that is on average in the early fifties, but somewhere between the mid-forties and mid-fifties is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many changes that people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changes in sleep and in mood, often already begin here, while you are still having periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and goes differently for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything after that 12-month line. Some symptoms decrease over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of an operation in which the ovaries are removed, some cancer treatments or other conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), and it is good to discuss that with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, a doctor recognises perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. It is done sooner if someone is younger or if the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do: honestly keep track of what you notice, such as waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of warmth, often in your face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, palpitations or a cold chill afterwards. Night sweats are the same during your sleep, and can be so strong that you wake up from it or your sheets get soaked.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few mild ones; others have many per day, which disrupt work and sleep. In some they disappear within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or heavy bedding. That differs greatly per person, and that is why keeping track of your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or you also have weight loss, fever or feel ill, tell a doctor.

**Describing them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many per day and per night, roughly
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to precede them
- What you have tried, and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Wave button and the after-the-fact log are there to record exactly this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatments, plus practical approaches. Which ones suit you, you discuss with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or HST) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces less of around menopause. Major guidelines call it an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**There are different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. Anyone who still has a uterus usually gets a progestogen prescribed as well as estrogen, to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long ago periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, a stroke or heart disease), and the type of treatment and the way it is administered. That is why you decide about this together with a doctor who knows your history; it is not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and which form is advisable, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how quickly?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not being treated?
- What should I watch for, and when do we review it again?

**If you already use it,** note it in MenoMap (You → Medication). MenoMap shows you your waves from before and after the start, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never recommends starting a medication, stopping it or changing it.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer another route. Those exist too, several in fact.

**Prescription options.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they reduce hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer group designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body approaches.** For cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause, there is evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that help people:**
- Layers that you can take off quickly
- A fan on your desk and next to your bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular exercise and a fixed sleep rhythm

**Supplements and herbal remedies.** For many of them the evidence is mixed or limited, quality differs, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you use, including products without a prescription.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before and during a change, and that is easier to judge than a feeling.

Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People often mainly remember the last days or the worst one. A simple overview fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not only that they are there
- Whether it is getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around it: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap revolves around a one-tap Wave button and an evening check-in with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a filled notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually gives a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything you are worried about. The Appointment tab in MenoMap helps you choose your questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
If you have not had a period for 12 months, then **any vaginal bleeding must be checked by a doctor**, even if it only happened once, and even if it was only spotting or light pink or brown discharge.

Usually the cause turns out not to be serious. The thinning of the lining of the vagina or the uterus, for example, is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much more treatable if it is discovered early. That is why official health guidelines say you should have it checked rather than wait and see.

**If you use hormone therapy,** a certain pattern of bleeding may be expected, depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, is heavier than normal or comes at the wrong time must also be checked.

**What you can do:**
- Contact your doctor or care provider and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, how much it was and what else you noticed. MenoMap can store this for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. The app reminds you to have it checked and includes it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most common complaints in middle age, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you straight away, or leave you lying too warm or too clammy to settle again.

**Other common factors:**
- Having to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol: with it you may fall asleep more easily, but the second half of the night often becomes more restless
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a snoring partner
- Snoring or breathing pauses, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (good to discuss, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What often helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can take off; a fixed time of getting up; and less alcohol right before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-researched approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What you can track.** For a week or two note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and wave log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When you should have it checked.** Talk to a doctor if sleeping badly affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice that your breathing stops at night or that you gasp for air.
